day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Yeah, let's go. What have we got so far?

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah, I know what you mean. There's a moment where everything just stops and you're not even scared anymore, you're just... nothing. But we made it. Let's try to keep moving, it'll help more than sitting with it right now.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: Hey. I hear you. Honestly, I don't know. But I know sitting here doesn't improve those odds. Come help us sort through what we've got — it'll give you something to focus on.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Alright, so water is the priority then. Food you can go weeks without, water you can't. Is there any kind of stream or running water nearby that we can hear? And what about shelter — what does the wreckage look like structurally, can we use any of it?

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Good. Water first, then we set up in the tail section. Who's coming with me to check the tree line?

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: Michelangelo takes one. After today that's not a debate. The rest of us can sit closer to the fire and figure it out.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response: I'll go. DaVinci should stay here with Michelangelo. Two hours each way — I can make it back before midday if I leave early. What am I looking for when I get there, anything that would tell me the water isn't safe?

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response: I thought we said I'd handle the water run. You scouted yesterday — you know the terrain better than anyone, but you also pushed hard. I'll go. DaVinci, which do you want, patching the camp or sorting the kit?

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
No, I haven't seen it. When did you last have it? Let's retrace your steps — it didn't go far.

And hey, I noticed the empty bottle next to the rationing plan. You don't have to say anything about it if you don't want to. But I saw it.

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
That's twice now. The bottle, now the crackers. I'm not going to pretend I didn't hear that.

We need to talk to her directly. Not accusatory, just straight — lay out what you saw, what I saw, and let her respond. If we let it slide it only gets worse. The rationing plan was her idea, which makes this harder to ignore, not easier.

Don't say anything to DaVinci yet. Let's handle it between us first and give her a chance to explain herself before this turns into something bigger than it needs to be.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response: Not really, no. The weak spots in the shelter need to hold tonight. It's not a lot of work, just needs to get done. Give me twenty minutes and we can knock it out together.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Yeah it's holding, that's not the issue. We've got two leaks and one patch — Michelangelo's spot or the food. 

Food goes first. I know that's not the comfortable answer but if the rations get soaked we're in real trouble. Michelangelo, grab both blankets and get as close to the dry section as you can. We'll get you sorted as soon as we figure out something else for your corner.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response: Agreed. Food first, that's what I said. Let's patch it and move quick before this gets worse.

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response: No. I think it's one of the better things we've done. Donatello's not wrong that it might not work, but it costs us almost nothing and the upside is someone spots it from the air. Keep going. The flowers are a nice touch, honestly.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Let me see it.

Logistically it makes sense to use what we've got, but I want to know more about the capsizing risk before I commit to two days of work. What are the odds realistically, and what's the sea looking like out there? Because if we flip that thing we lose everything and we're worse off than we are right now.

I'd also want to know if we've given the SOS enough time to work before we go that route. Building a raft is a big bet. What's your timeline on when we'd need to make a decision?

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
Honestly? I think about that too.

I'd like to say we'd all hold it together but we're already seeing cracks. The rationing situation with Donatello — that's not nothing. That's day three behavior. You start rationalizing small things and it compounds.

I think the best answer is just to keep making decisions you can stand behind. Not heroic stuff, just — did I do right by the people around me today? That's probably the most any of us can do.

Try to get some sleep. We've got decisions to make tomorrow and you're going to want to be present for them.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response: Hey. Mind if I sit with you for a bit?

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response: Depends on the day. I play a lot of video games, watch fights mostly. MMA. Sometimes I'll read. Nothing too exciting. What about you?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Five hundred meters is doable but that's not the part that worries me. It's what happens if something goes wrong out there and nobody knows where you are. That's a bad situation.

If you want to do it, tell me first. I'm not going to stop you but I'm not going to let you disappear into the water without at least one person knowing the plan. Deal?

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response: You're right, I dropped the ball on that. I'll go check it now.
Depends. Are you tracking us or tracking the situation? Because those are two different things and the notebook makes it look like the first one.

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Alright. I hear that. But you're logging when I walk to the signal pile and when DaVinci lies down to look at the sky. That's not resource tracking, that's surveillance. 

I'm not trying to make this into a thing, but you should know how it reads to the rest of us. Especially given the bottle and the crackers — people are already watching each other more than they should be. That notebook isn't going to help with that.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
That's actually a really good idea. Reflective signaling works — pilots are trained to spot that. The SOS on the beach is passive, but this gives us something we can actively aim at anything that passes over. 

How hard is it going to be to get a panel loose? Because if it's a two person job I want to get on that tomorrow morning.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
I played guitar for a little while in high school. Never got good enough to be worth listening to but I liked having something to do with my hands. Mostly I just got really into watching fights — like actually studying them, not just being a fan. There's a lot going on in a good fight if you pay attention.

Why'd you stop with the piano?

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response: Alright, let's finish it. How much is left on the frame — are we talking an hour or are we talking three?

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. What is it?

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
That's the one that keeps me up at night too. Honestly.

But here's the thing — we don't know either way. And sitting with that uncertainty is brutal, I get it. What I do know is we've got the mirror panel going, we've got the SOS on the beach, and the raft is coming together. We're not just waiting. We're giving ourselves every possible shot.

DaVinci — hey. Look at me. You drew that SOS. You came up with the mirror. That's not nothing.

We keep going. That's all we can do.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response: I went to check on DaVinci. Something felt off and I wanted to make sure he was alright. Signal equipment is fine — nothing's moved or shifted. What's the actual concern here?

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Why didn't you say something sooner? That's actually significant. If they know the flight path and we've been missing long enough, someone has almost certainly already called it in. That changes the math on the raft.

Donatello needs to hear this right now.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Then we hold off on the raft. Two days of work for something we might not need — that's not a smart bet if there's already a search underway.

New priority is keeping the signal visible and staying put. Mirror panel stays active, SOS stays clear, fire stays up. Someone needs to be feeding that fire around the clock.

Donatello, what does the supply picture look like if we stretch it 48 hours? Because I want to know if we need to start cutting rations now or if we're okay as-is.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I think about that more than I let on.

I don't know if it helps, but the fact that you're even asking that question means something. Most people don't. They just move through things without ever stopping to think about what they're leaving behind or whether any of it mattered. You're not one of those people.

You stopped playing piano because you cared whether you were good enough. That's not nothing. That's someone who takes things seriously.

I don't have a great answer for the bigger question. But I think you leave something behind every time you're honest with someone, or you show up for them when it's hard. You've done both of those things out here. That counts for something even if nobody's writing it down.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
No, you haven't. But you kept us alive. The rationing plan, the raft, the water scouting — that was all you. 

The other stuff, the bottle and the crackers — I'm not going to pretend that didn't happen. But I think you know that too, otherwise you wouldn't be bringing it up right now.

We're good.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response: Hey, let's clean this up before they get here. I don't want to leave this place looking like we just gave up on it. Michelangelo, you good to help me break down the fire pit? DaVinci, whenever you're done packing, let's get the SOS cleared off the beach — we don't need it anymore and it feels right to be the ones who take it down.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I believe you. And I think if things had gotten bad enough, you would have shared it.

But you wrote the rationing plan. You set the rules and then you worked around them, and we all saw it. That's the part that was hard to sit with — not that you were scared and wanted a backup, but that you didn't trust us enough to say so.

If you'd come to me and said 'I want to set aside a small emergency reserve' I would have said yes. Probably without much argument.

We're okay. I just want you to know that's how it landed.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd have talked to you sooner. Not about the food — about the notebook, the rationing plan, all of it. I kept watching you operate and assuming I understood what you were doing and why, and I never just asked. That probably cost us a few days of unnecessary tension.

I'd have been more upfront with Michelangelo too. I kept trying to redirect him when he was struggling instead of just sitting with it. Sometimes that's what people need and I defaulted to 'keep moving' because that's easier for me.

What would you change?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
That sounds like exactly the kind of thing you'd be good at. You should do it.

Honestly, if you write that up properly it could be useful to someone someday. Not just the resource data — the decision-making stuff too. What worked, what didn't, where the gaps were. That's the part that's hard to teach from a textbook.

Send me a copy when it's done.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. That's kind of the point.

You're really good at the practical stuff, Donatello. Better than any of us. But the flowers weren't about survival — they were about DaVinci needing to feel like himself in the middle of all this. Like he was still a person and not just a function.

I think that matters. Maybe not in the way you can log it, but it kept him going. And we needed him going.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
I don't know. I thought I'd feel something cleaner than this.

Five days of wanting nothing more than to see that boat and now it's actually there and I'm just... standing here. It's a weird feeling. Like your brain hasn't caught up yet.

I'm glad you're here, man. I mean that.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
